title: AESTHETICS, AFFECT, AND COGNITION Environmental Preference from an Evolutionary Perspective
central_proposition: Environmental preference is an intuitive, rapid, and often unconscious guide to behavior, rooted in evolutionary adaptation, that involves complex information processing to assess environmental affordances for understanding and exploration, thereby influencing human experience and behavior.

concept_definitions.name: Mystery
concept_definitions.definition: The promise that more information could be gained by moving deeper into a depicted setting, inferred from what is present in the scene but not immediately visible.

concept_definitions.name: Coherence
concept_definitions.definition: The capacity to predict within a scene, reflecting the ease with which information can be organized into a relatively small number of chunks, contributing to a 'good gestalt'.

concept_definitions.name: Understanding
concept_definitions.definition: An affectively important informational outcome related to comprehending or making sense of a scene.

concept_definitions.name: Exploration
concept_definitions.definition: An affectively important informational outcome related to being held by a setting, or being attracted by or pulled toward sources of additional information.

concept_definitions.name: Legibility
concept_definitions.definition: The inferred capacity to continue to comprehend the environment and maintain orientation in space as one moves deeper into a scene, allowing prediction and orientation beyond the immediate view.

concept_definitions.name: Affordance
concept_definitions.definition: The implicit analysis of the function an object or environment might serve for an individual, focusing on what the environment offers the perceiving organism.

concept_definitions.name: Primary Landscape Qualities
concept_definitions.definition: Certain environmental contents (e.g., water, trees, foliage) that have a special, strong effect on preference due to their indications of properties that support human life.

concept_definitions.name: Prospect
concept_definitions.definition: Having a grand view or an overview of the landscape, providing an informational advantage.

concept_definitions.name: Refuge
concept_definitions.definition: Having a safe place to hide, a place from which one can see without being seen, providing a safety advantage.

concept_definitions.name: Agoraphobia (as a predictor)
concept_definitions.definition: The discomfort associated with wide open areas largely lacking in protective cover, acting as a negative predictor of preference.

argument_structure: The paper begins by critiquing existing environmental preference research for its theoretical void and fragmented efforts. It then introduces a conceptual framework based on two informational outcomes (Understanding and Exploration) and two temporal dimensions (immediate vs. inferred information), yielding four key predictors (Coherence, Complexity, Legibility, Mystery). This framework is then interpreted through an evolutionary lens, proposing that preference serves as an adaptive, intuitive guide to behavior. Finally, the paper integrates these ideas to offer a new perspective on the cognition-affect relationship, arguing for a spectrum of interactions rather than a dichotomy, and highlighting the pervasive role of aesthetics.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core mechanism posits that humans rapidly and unconsciously process environmental information to make predictions about its potential for 'Understanding' (comprehension, orientation) and 'Exploration' (new information, engagement). These predictions, along with the presence of 'primary landscape qualities' (e.g., water, foliage) indicative of life-supporting habitats, are immediately translated into an 'affective code' (preference). This affective response then intuitively guides behavior, drawing individuals towards environments that are adaptively beneficial (e.g., safe, resource-rich, easy to navigate, offering opportunities for learning) and away from unpromising ones. This process is seen as an evolved, efficient, and economical mechanism for survival and adaptation, often operating below conscious awareness.

findings.mechanism: Content of the environment (e.g., natural vs. built) has a special status in human reactions, leading to differential aesthetic responses.
findings.source: Research on Preference: The Emergence of a Framework
findings.quote: Natural scenes were so uniformly preferred over scenes of the built environment that only a single built environment scene (an urban park) was as preferred as the lowest rated natural scene.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Kaplan et al. (1972) found natural scenes overwhelmingly preferred over built scenes.

findings.mechanism: These variables represent different aspects of information processing related to 'Understanding' (Coherence, Legibility) and 'Exploration' (Complexity, Mystery), which are fundamental to assessing an environment's utility and appeal.
findings.quote: In this way three candidate variables were identified: Complexity, Mystery, and Coherence.
findings.empirical_support_cited: R. Kaplan (1973) demonstrated Coherence and Mystery as important predictors. Subsequent studies supported Mystery and Coherence, with varying support for Complexity and Legibility.

findings.mechanism: Mystery implies the promise of additional information, enticing individuals to explore and update their cognitive maps, which is adaptively beneficial.
findings.quote: The scenes appeared to promise that more information could be gained by moving deeper into the depicted setting. This promise of additional information tentatively was labeled 'Mystery.'
findings.empirical_support_cited: Kaplan et al. (1972) identified Mystery in highly preferred scenes. Subsequent studies found strong support for Mystery as a predictor.

findings.antecedent: Coherence (ease of organizing information, predictability within scene)
findings.mechanism: Coherence aids comprehension and reduces cognitive load, making an environment easier to understand and navigate, which is adaptively beneficial.
findings.quote: The underlying informational theme in Coherence is the capacity to predict within the scene. The ease with which the information in the scene can be organized into a relatively small number of chunks is the central issue here.
findings.empirical_support_cited: R. Kaplan (1973) demonstrated Coherence as an important predictor. Subsequent studies provided strong support for its predictive role.

findings.antecedent: Legibility (inference of continued comprehension and orientation deeper in scene)
findings.mechanism: Legibility ensures that an individual can maintain orientation and avoid getting lost when moving through an environment, which is crucial for survival and efficient navigation.
findings.quote: Legibility concerns the inference that being able to predict and to maintain orientation will be possible as one wanders more deeply into the scene.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Woodcock (1982) found Legibility to be a strong predictor, especially interacting with Mystery and Primary Prospect.

findings.consequent: Conscious awareness of underlying cognitive processes
findings.mechanism: Preference judgments are rapid and automatic, reflecting an intuitive, unconscious assessment of environmental affordances, similar to habitat selection in animals, where the adaptive basis is not consciously articulated.
findings.quote: participants are generally unable to explain their choices. They tend to be quite unaware of the variables that proved so effective in predicting what they would prefer.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Participants made preference judgments rapidly and easily but were generally unable to explain their choices or the variables influencing them.

findings.mechanism: An evolutionary bias for the savanna biome, believed to be the environment in which humans evolved, is most evident at a young age before familiarity and cultural learning exert a strong influence.
findings.quote: the younger children's decided preference for savanna, the environment in which the human species is believed to have evolved, is consistent with an evolutionary interpretation.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Balling and Falk (1982) found young children (8- and 11-year-olds) showed a substantial preference for savanna over other biomes.

findings.mechanism: Having a grand view provides an adaptive advantage by offering an overview of the landscape, facilitating information gathering and threat detection.
findings.quote: Prospect refers to having a grand view, an overview, as it were, of the landscape.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Woodcock (1982) found Primary Prospect to be a strong predictor.

findings.antecedent: Refuge (safe place to hide, see without being seen)
findings.mechanism: Refuge provides a sense of safety and security, which is adaptively beneficial, but its effect on preference is complex and context-dependent, as being too enclosed (e.g., deep in woods) can be dispreferred.
findings.quote: Refuge refers to having a safe place to hide, a place from which one can see without being seen.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Woodcock (1982) found Primary Refuge (view from cover) was a negative predictor, while the combination of Primary Refuge and Agoraphobia suggested preference for forest edges.

findings.mechanism: Mystery and Legibility interact synergistically; a scene that promises new information (Mystery) and also ensures continued orientation (Legibility) is highly preferred because it offers both exploration and safety, optimizing adaptive benefits.
findings.quote: Mystery and Legibility interact such that a high-Mystery, high-Legibility scene is even more preferred than would be expected given the independent contribution of these variables.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Woodcock (1982) found Mystery and Legibility interact such that a high-Mystery, high-Legibility scene is even more preferred than expected.

findings.mechanism: The presence of a grand vista (Primary Prospect) can be so engaging that it overrides the need for explicit Legibility, but in its absence, Legibility becomes critical for practical navigation and avoiding getting lost.
findings.quote: A high-Primary Prospect scene will tend to be preferred whether it is legible or not, but preference for a scene low in Primary Prospect is dependent upon Legibility.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Woodcock (1982) found Primary Prospect and Legibility interact in a different fashion: high-Primary Prospect scenes are preferred regardless of Legibility, but low-Primary Prospect scenes depend on Legibility.

findings.mechanism: Neither being fully exposed (agoraphobia) nor deeply hidden in dense woods (Primary Refuge) is preferred; the optimal balance for safety, resources, and information gathering is found at the forest edge, which is adaptively significant.
findings.quote: When the Primary Refuge and Agoraphobia results are combined it becomes clear that neither being out in the open nor being in the woods is favored. These opposing vectors would tend to place the individual right at the forest edge.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Woodcock (1982) found Primary Refuge was a negative predictor, and Agoraphobia was a significant negative predictor. Their combined results suggest preference for the forest edge.

findings.mechanism: Different environmental predictors require varying degrees and types of cognitive processing; Mystery, for instance, requires complex, inferential, and often unconscious processing to construct a conceptual model of space and simulate locomotion.
findings.source: Cognition and Affect from the Perspective of Environmental Aesthetics
findings.quote: Mystery seems to call upon a reasonably complex, albeit unconscious, inferential process.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Null (purely theoretical argument based on the nature of the predictors)

findings.antecedent: Rapid, automatic prediction of environmental informational possibilities
findings.consequent: Adaptive behavior (orientation, access to new information)
findings.mechanism: A quick, unconscious assessment of an environment's affordances (e.g., for navigation, learning) allows for rapid reevaluation and response, keeping the individual in an adaptively favorable state and guiding locomotion.
findings.source: A Hypothesis Concerning Environmental Preference in the Ongoing Function of the Individual
findings.quote: In this way preference would help keep the individual in an environment in which orientation and access to new information can be maintained easily-quite apart from the particular purposes that the individual was pursuing at that moment.

findings.mechanism: The knowledge of being in the presence of 'primary landscape qualities' that indicate life-supporting habitats triggers a rapid cognitive reaction with affective concomitants, which is adaptively beneficial.
findings.source: A Hypothesis Concerning Environmental Preference in the Ongoing Function of the Individual
findings.quote: The operative factor here is the knowledge and not merely the visual pattern on which it is based. In other words, knowing that one is in the presence of such contents seems to have a strong impact.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Null (theoretical argument, though earlier studies identified these as 'primary landscape qualities')

findings.mechanism: Aesthetics, as an expression of intuitive, unconscious inclinations, serves as a pervasive guide that influences choices and actions not only in the physical environment but potentially in other domains, reflecting a fundamental adaptive function.
findings.quote: Aesthetics could thus be seen as a set of inclinations, however intuitive or unconscious, which might influence the direction people choose not only in the physical environment but also in other domains.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: The relative weighting of Coherence, Complexity, Legibility, and Mystery in predicting preference will vary depending on the specific environmental content (e.g., urban vs. rural, different biomes).
The interaction effects between Mystery and Legibility, and between Primary Prospect and Legibility, on preference can be empirically verified across different environmental settings.

Physiological and behavioral responses (e.g., approach/avoidance, gaze patterns) will correlate with preference judgments, even when participants cannot consciously articulate the reasons for their choices.

Exposure to environments combining high 'Understanding' and 'Exploration' potential, along with 'primary landscape qualities,' will lead to faster stress recovery and improved cognitive performance compared to less preferred environments.
The preference for forest-edge environments (balancing refuge and prospect, avoiding agoraphobia) can be empirically tested through choice experiments and physiological measures.
bridge_warrants: The paper connects its framework to Zajonc's (1980) cognition-affect debate, arguing for a spectrum of relationships rather than a dichotomy, where complex, unconscious cognition can precede affect.
It draws parallels between its 'implicit analysis of function' and Gibson's (1979) concept of 'affordance,' emphasizing what the environment offers the perceiving organism.
The concept of Legibility is explicitly linked to Lynch's (1960) work on urban legibility, extending it to natural environments and inferential spatial understanding.
The evolutionary interpretation of preference is supported by animal habitat selection literature (Wecker, 1964; Woodcock, 1982) and Appleton's (1975) Prospect-Refuge theory.
The discussion of complexity and its inverted-U relationship builds upon and critiques Berlyne's (1960) collative variables, suggesting a more nuanced role for complexity in real-world environments.
methodological_critiques: The paper criticizes previous environmental preference research for a 'disturbing theoretical void' and a tendency towards 'fragmentary, unrelated research efforts' (Zube et al., 1982).

It notes that earlier studies using randomly generated visual stimuli (e.g., Berlyne's collative variables) were less representative and failed to capture the importance of content in real-world environments.

The initial definition of 'Legibility' was problematic, leading judges to award high scores to desolate open spaces, necessitating a modification to include 'being able to get back again' for better predictive power.

The paper implicitly critiques the common assumption that cognition is necessarily a conscious calculational process, advocating for a broader understanding of cognitive processes that can be unconscious.
model_structure: The core model is a 2x2 matrix (Table 1) categorizing environmental predictors of preference based on two informational outcomes: 'Understanding' and 'Exploration,' and two temporal dimensions of information availability: 'Immediate' and 'Inferred/Predicted.' This yields four key predictors: Coherence (Immediate/Understanding), Complexity (Immediate/Exploration), Legibility (Predicted/Understanding), and Mystery (Predicted/Exploration). This framework is then integrated with evolutionary principles and a nuanced view of cognition-affect interaction.
limitations: The paper acknowledges that the theoretical framework is 'obviously still incomplete and in need of refinement.'
It notes that the concept of Legibility initially received little support and required further development to become an effective predictor.

The paper implicitly acknowledges the complexity of cultural and genetic interactions, suggesting that evolutionary biases might be modulated by environmental context (e.g., Eskimos in contrasting environments).

paper_metadata.title: Aesthetics, Affect, and Cognition
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Scenes of the outdoor physical environment vary substantially in the extent to which they are preferred. Variables empirically found to predict preference can be analyzed both in terms of their information-processing implications and in terms of their evolutionary significance. Some of these predictors appear to require fairly extensive information processing, thus supporting the hypothesis that a rapid, unconscious type of cognition may precede certain affective judgments. Such ties between cognition and affect are understandable in the context of the proposed theoretical framework for environmental preference. This framework not only provides a coherent guide to research but also points to the pervasiveness and significance of aesthetics as a factor in human behavior and human experience.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Human preferences for certain natural environments are rooted in adaptive responses to ancestral environments, promoting survival and well-being by signaling safety, resources, and opportunities for restoration.
Exposure to certain natural environments can reduce physiological and psychological stress, leading to restoration from negative affective states and contributing to preference.

mechanism_chain.description: A psycho-evolutionary mechanism linking specific environmental features to immediate affective and physiological responses, which in turn drive environmental preference.

steps.from_construct: Environmental features (e.g., presence of water, vegetation, open vistas, moderate complexity, absence of threats)
steps.to_construct: Perception of evolutionary significance (e.g., safety, resource availability, refuge, threat)
Immediate affective responses (e.g., pleasure, calmness, interest, fear)
Physiological responses (e.g., stress reduction, changes in arousal)

steps.from_construct: Positive affective and physiological responses (e.g., stress reduction, restoration)
